signal.rationale: OP frames the bond yield breakout as the macro trade; long-duration shorts implied

clips.text_en_b2: US Treasury yields are breaking out yet again, with the 2-year, 10-year, and 30-year all grinding higher in tandem. Basis points across the curve keep widening, and the long-anticipated Fed cut is being priced in, then systematically unpriced. Term premium has been the buzzword on /biz/ all evening, and oil is being floated as the next supercycle play. One anon put it bluntly: loading up on digital IOUs while bond yields rip higher is a genuinely wild call.
clips.text_en_c1: US Treasury yields have resumed their upward trajectory across the entire curve, with the 2-year, 10-year, and 30-year all grinding higher in tandem. Basis point spreads between tenors are widening once again, suggesting that the recently priced-in Fed cut is now being systematically unpriced. Term premium, a term that has been worn thin on /biz/, is back at the centre of the macro discourse. Oil is meanwhile being floated as the foundation of an emerging supercycle. As one anonymous commentator wryly observed, accumulating digital IOUs while sovereign yields break out constitutes a particularly audious allocation decision.
clips.text_en_c2: US Treasury yields have broken out decisively once more, with the 2-year, 10-year, and 30-year benchmarks all grinding higher in lockstep. Basis point spreads across the curve are widening rather than compressing, which is precisely the configuration that unsettles anyone with duration risk. Markets had largely priced in a Fed cut; that expectation is now being unwound almost in real time, and the term premium, long dismissed as a tired talking point, has clawed its way back into the conversation on /biz/ overnight. Layered on top is chatter that oil may be entering a fresh supercycle, an unusually combustible combination when real yields are already rising. One anonymous poster captured the absurdity rather neatly: accumulating digital IOUs while sovereign yields break out constitutes, in his words, a singularly unhinged allocation decision.

clips.text_en_c2: Anthropic has reportedly informed investors that the company has achieved operating profitability, although that feat obtains only once one excises model training expenditure and the revenue-sharing arrangements with partners such as Amazon from the equation. Adjusted operating income is projected to remain positive for a further quarter, with gross margins comfortably clearing eighty per cent before those particular line items are reintroduced. The framing has, predictably, drawn accusations of creative accounting from a sceptical audience, including engineers on /g/ who read the disclosure less as triumph than as a deliberate sleight of hand. Beneath the celebratory press release lies the more uncomfortable question of how sustainable a business model truly is when its headline profitability is contingent upon excluding its single largest cost category. The subtext, for anyone paying attention, is rather less flattering.

clips.text_zh: OpenAI 又柒⋯⋯ 俾人發現 desktop app 嘅 GPT-6 Astra selector 其實 route 去 GPT-5.5。Peak hour 美國 traffic 就會 trigger edge classifier，靜靜雞 shunt 去舊 model。Scam Altman 又贏一波 🧐 我自己都用緊，真係靠 AI 續命（廢物mode）。
clips.text_en_b1: OpenAI got caught fake-routing GPT-6 Astra to GPT-5.5 on desktop. Astra is advertised at $20 a month, with a knowledge cutoff of April 2026. But a raw diagnostic probe with no tool calls returned December 2025 as the cutoff. So the desktop model selector is basically decorative. During peak US traffic, low-perplexity prompts get quietly shunted to the older model.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread with proof that GPT-6 Astra is silently served from a quantized GPT-5.5

signal.rationale: No trade setup, just an AI product oddity

clips.text_en_b2: OpenAI has been caught red-handed routing GPT-6 Astra requests to GPT-5.5 on desktop. Astra is marketed at $20 a month with an April 2026 knowledge cutoff, yet a raw diagnostic probe with no tool calls returned December 2025 instead. The model selector is basically decorative, because during peak US traffic an edge classifier quietly shunts low-perplexity prompts to the older model. Sam Altman strikes again, and paying subscribers are essentially beta-testers without realising it.
clips.text_en_c1: OpenAI has once again found itself at the centre of controversy after investigative users discovered that the desktop application's GPT-6 Astra selector is, in practice, routing queries to the considerably older GPT-5.5 model. Astra is marketed at twenty dollars monthly with a stated knowledge cutoff of April 2026; however, a raw diagnostic probe devoid of tool calls returned December 2025 as the operative threshold. The selector function appears largely cosmetic. During peak American traffic hours, prompts exhibiting lower perplexity scores are quietly redirected to legacy infrastructure, a practice that strikes many subscribers as fundamentally deceptive.
clips.text_en_c2: OpenAI has once again been caught in a rather unedifying deception, one that would be considered embarrassing were it not so transparently cynical. Reverse engineers discovered that the desktop application's GPT-6 Astra selector, marketed at twenty dollars monthly with a knowledge horizon of April 2026, is in fact routing queries to GPT-5.5 whenever backend classifiers deem it prudent. A raw diagnostic probe containing no tool invocations returned December 2025 as the operative cutoff, suggesting that the model picker is essentially ornamental. During peak American traffic, prompts registering low perplexity are quietly shunted onto the inferior model, a manoeuvre that spares OpenAI's expensive inference capacity while charging subscribers premium rates for a service they are not, strictly speaking, receiving. The episode will not damage the company's standing with the investment community, though it ought to.

clips.text_en_c1: The United States has, for the first time, formally confirmed the deployment of weapons in space, a revelation that has prompted immediate and pointed responses from both China and Russia. clips.text_en_c2: The United States has, for the first time, formally acknowledged the deployment of weapons in orbit, a disclosure that elicited immediate and pointed responses from both Beijing and Moscow. CBS News is leading its broadcast with the story, while /pol/ has correctly identified it as a meaningful escalation in an already strained geopolitical environment. From a market perspective, the headline functions as a textbook risk-off catalyst: gold and crude ought to find bids on any sustained deterioration in sentiment, whilst defence primes and pure-play space equities may attract capital seeking convex exposure to the new posture. Whether the admission is intended as deterrence signalling or as genuine policy revelation remains ambiguous; what is unambiguous is that adversaries will calibrate accordingly, and that the marginal allocation decision for the foreseeable quarter has become marginally more complicated.

clips.text_en_c2: After a full month away from the platform, an anonymous poster returned to the deadlift and proceeded to hoist 220 kilograms for a clean double, convinced upon completion that further repetitions had remained within his grasp. His all-time personal record stands at 240 kilograms, and he contends, with the quiet confidence of someone accustomed to the barbell, that his working strength has since improved materially. At home he had been sustaining his training with kettlebell clean and press, an adequate but unsatisfying substitute, and the urge to pull genuinely heavy iron had become, by his own admission, rather difficult to ignore. He concedes, with the benefit of hindsight, that an ambitious 245 or even 250 kilogram attempt ought to have been on the menu.

clips.text_en_c1: While contemporary seasonal anime productions continue to proliferate at an overwhelming pace, a growing contingent on /a/ has been rediscovering the considerable merits of revisiting mid-2000s classics. One anonymous poster recently curated a rotation comprising Hellsing, Wolf's Rain, Bleach, and Azumanga Daioh, prompting broader discussion regarding forgotten favourites. There is something distinctly affecting about revisiting series that originally aired during one's formative years, a nostalgic resonance that newer works, however accomplished, rarely replicate. The thread has since evolved into a sprawling communal exercise in collective reminiscence, with contributors trading recommendations that span nearly two decades of animation history.
clips.text_en_c2: Contemporary seasonal anime remains a perfectly serviceable form of entertainment, yet there persists a peculiar gravitational pull exerted by the catalogue of the early millennium, a phenomenon that resists easy articulation. One anonymous enthusiast has lately devoted his evenings to revisiting that exact corpus, with Hellsing, Wolf's Rain, Bleach, and Azumanga Daioh comprising his present rotation, each title bearing the unmistakable patina of a decade that took itself neither too seriously nor too lightly. The thread on /a/ has duly solicited recommendations from the assembled readership, though the more revealing subtext concerns the manner in which works produced during one's formative years acquire, upon revisitation, a density of meaning that subsequent releases struggle to replicate. The current slate of new productions, for all its polish, lacks the particular texture that nostalgia alone can confer.
